surface_forms: la madame de Sainte-Euverte que j'avais connue
Mme de Sainte-Euverte de La Rochefoucauld

appraisal_events.evidence: « ces positions en apparence imprenables du duc et de la duchesse de Guermantes... avaient perdu leur inviolabilité » ; « Ne pouvant se passer d'Odette » ; « le vieux fauve dompté... rentrait dans ses épaules sa tête » ; « c'est en un personnage de Molière — non pas même en l'olympien amant d'Alcmène mais en un risible Géronte — que se change inévitablement Jupiter ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator stages the collapse of the duke's supposedly impregnable position: installed as a dependent fixture in Mme de Forcheville's drawing room, he backs down before her stare like a caged animal and is deceived without seeing it, the Jupiter/Géronte comparison sealing the diminishment as the narrator's own judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Aussi la duchesse était-elle fort malheureuse » ; « La duchesse avait toujours été un peu menteuse et l'était devenue davantage » ; « elle suivait la mode, bien qu'avec quelque retard » ; « même à sa défense de l'actualité, la duchesse mêlait ses préjugés d'aristocrate » (on Gilberte: « ce n'est même pas une femme, c'est ce que je connais de plus factice et de plus bourgeois au monde »).
appraisal_events.explanation: The closing movement lowers Oriane from within: she is unhappy and policed by her husband, caught denying a past the narrator knows, and her contemptuous verdicts on Gilberte, the Sainte-Euverte and Bréauté are framed as belated fashion-following plus aristocratic prejudice rather than the discernment she once embodied.

status_effects.explanation: His Faubourg position is explicitly declared to have lost its inviolability; he no longer appears in the duchess's salon and holds forth instead as a curiosity before a cocotte's guests, in the cage rather than the desert.
The narrator turns his former thunder into risible senility — dulled sight, hearing and vigilance, Jupiter degraded into a Molière Géronte.
She gains clear local leverage: she holds the duke's ferocious gaze until he yields, he cannot do without her, and she rejoins other men the moment he leaves without his daring to notice.

The same sequence withholds any elevation of her worth: her interruptions have little sense, the narrator calls her « médiocre dans ce rôle comme dans tous les autres », and her staged frankness about Swann is known by him to be mixed with lies.
She is exposed as an increasingly habitual liar with derivative, fashion-lagging taste, her worldly contempt reduced to snobbery she once would have mocked.
She is « fort malheureuse », her husband reserving his thunderbolts for her alone while Mme de Forcheville feeds his irritation against her.

Within the duchess's speech Gilberte is dismissed as unworthy company, artificial and bourgeois; the local snub carries real social force even though the narrator marks the verdict as aristocratic prejudice rather than endorsing it.

ambiguities: « Mme de Sainte-Euverte » denotes two distinct people here: the young woman on the chaise longue (wife of a grand-nephew, née La Rochefoucauld), listed unresolved under the passage's surface form, and the older marquise de Saint-Euverte of the reference sheet, whose fallen salon the duchess likes to disown.

Odette's local movement is genuinely two-directional: she masters the duke and deceives him at will while the narrator simultaneously denies her any distinction, so her ascendancy is recorded as leverage rather than elevation.

Charlus's claim that the duchess's legend of purity conceals countless affairs is left explicitly undecided by the narrator (« Entre ces deux idées je ne pouvais décider »); it is therefore not treated as an established discredit, only as part of the passage's general unsettling of her standing.
